enlightenment-ideas-and-natural-rights.title: Enlightenment Ideas and Natural Rights
enlightenment-ideas-and-natural-rights.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate enlightenment ideas and natural rights?
paragraphs: Locke's social-contract arguments challenged unlimited monarchy by asking why political authority is legitimate. Natural-rights reasoning holds that certain rights do not depend on a ruler's gift, while consent of the governed requires government to answer to the people. Enlightenment authors disagreed about representation, property, religion and who qualified as a political member. Their arguments should be studied in their historical context, including exclusions they did not remedy.

In an eighteenth-century petition, a community claims its ruler may tax them without considering their views. Compare this position with a consent-based argument: what would each side call a legitimate law? Distinguish Locke's ideas from the later government designed under the U.S. Constitution.

Use Declaration of Independence (1776) to identify the governing rule, then compare it with Constitution. Explain what these documents can establish, which group or institution is affected, and what additional evidence would test the results. the-declaration-of-independence.title: The Declaration of Independence
the-declaration-of-independence.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate the declaration of independence?
paragraphs: The Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Second Continental Congress in 1776. It states political principles concerning equality, rights, consent and the right to alter a destructive government. Its list of grievances makes an argument against British rule and addresses audiences at home and abroad. Unlike the Constitution, it did not create the operating branches of the later federal government.

Its broad language also existed alongside enslavement, unequal political participation and dispossession of Indigenous nations. A historian can recognize the significance of the Declaration's claims while investigating whose rights were protected in practice and whose perspectives were absent from the document.

the-principles-of-democratic-government.title: The Principles of Democratic Government
the-principles-of-democratic-government.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate the principles of democratic government?
paragraphs: Popular sovereignty places ultimate political authority in the people. Republican government uses representatives selected through established political rules, while constitutionalism limits the powers of public officials. The rule of law requires government action to follow legal constraints; it does not mean every law or decision is automatically fair. These principles can reinforce one another or come into tension.

A constitutional democracy requires more than counting votes: students must ask about rights, jurisdiction, judicial review and accountable procedures. Examine the difference between a principle proclaimed in a document and its implementation.

the-constitutional-convention.title: The Constitutional Convention
the-constitutional-convention.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate the constitutional convention?
paragraphs: Delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787 after difficulties under the Articles of Confederation. They debated representation, federal powers, slavery and the balance between national and state authority. The Connecticut Compromise helped create different representation rules for the House and Senate, while the Three-Fifths Clause strengthened slaveholding states' representation without granting enslaved people political rights.

The Constitution was written through negotiation and ratification disputes, not unanimous agreement about all problems. Women, enslaved people and most Indigenous nations were not delegates. Historians distinguish constitutional architecture from the unequal participation of the founding era.

federalism-and-separation-of-powers.title: Federalism and Separation of Powers
federalism-and-separation-of-powers.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate federalism and separation of powers?
paragraphs: Federalism divides responsibilities between national and state governments, while separation of powers distributes federal authority among legislative, executive and judicial branches. These are different arrangements. Congress legislates within constitutional authority; the president executes federal law; federal courts resolve cases within their jurisdiction.

Issues such as education, environmental regulation and public safety can involve overlapping jurisdictions. The Supremacy Clause gives valid federal law priority when it conflicts with state law, but not every federal policy is constitutionally authorized. The core inquiry is which level or branch has a particular power and why.

checks-and-balances.title: Checks and Balances
checks-and-balances.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate checks and balances?
paragraphs: Checks and balances give institutions ways to limit other institutions while performing their own assigned responsibilities. The president may veto legislation; Congress may override a veto by the required supermajority; the Senate exercises advice-and-consent powers for certain appointments and treaties. Courts may review governmental actions in cases properly before them.

A check can delay action, force negotiation or protect institutional boundaries. Students should identify the actual power, the actor using it and the conditions under which it operates. Political disagreements are not themselves proof of a constitutional crisis.

constitutional-change-and-interpretation.title: Constitutional Change and Interpretation
constitutional-change-and-interpretation.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate constitutional change and interpretation?
paragraphs: Article V creates an amendment process requiring substantial agreement across national and state institutions. Judicial interpretation through cases and constitutional practice can also influence how governmental powers and rights are applied, but interpretation is not the same process as formally changing the document's text.

The Reconstruction Amendments and later voting-rights amendments show how the Constitution changed over time. Each development emerged from political struggles involving unequal participation, competing ideas about citizenship and enforcement. Ask whether a proposed change requires an amendment, legislation or a judicial ruling.

paragraphs: Landmark cases are best studied through facts, constitutional question, holding and consequences. Brown v. the-bill-of-rights.title: The Bill of Rights
the-bill-of-rights.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate the bill of rights?

Most of these protections later became applicable to states through interpretation of the Fourteenth Amendment.

due-process-and-equal-protection.title: Due Process and Equal Protection
due-process-and-equal-protection.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate due process and equal protection?
paragraphs: The Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments contain due-process guarantees, while the Fourteenth Amendment also prohibits states from denying equal protection of the laws. Due process concerns fair legal procedures and, in particular contexts, substantive limits; equal protection concerns government's unequal treatment under constitutional standards.

A case about suspension, search, criminal charges or discriminatory policy needs careful analysis of who acted, what right is implicated and what process was afforded. Not every unfair outcome is automatically a proven constitutional violation.

civil-rights-through-constitutional-chan.title: Civil Rights Through Constitutional Change
civil-rights-through-constitutional-chan.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate civil rights through constitutional change?

how-american-elections-work.title: How American Elections Work
how-american-elections-work.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate how american elections work?

Voters choose members of Congress directly; presidential selection uses state-administered elections for electors under constitutional and legal rules. Eligibility, voter registration, polling and ballot procedures vary by jurisdiction and can change with law or court decisions.

Historical inquiry asks how protections and participation changed over time, not which party a learner should support.

citizen-participation-beyond-voting.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate citizen participation beyond voting?
paragraphs: Civic participation also includes attending public meetings, contacting representatives, joining community organizations, petitioning, volunteering and collaborating on local problems. Constitutional protections for speech and peaceful assembly interact with lawful time, place and manner rules in relevant settings.
